terms.gloss: money lent or borrowed: a loan
evidence: Cic. Att. 11.3.3: cui magnam dedimus pecūniam mūtuam, to whom I have lent a large sum
Caes. BC 1.39.3: mūtuās pecūniās sūmpsit, he borrowed money
terms.comment: Latin says it with mūtuus, lent: pecūniam mūtuam dare, to lend money, sūmere, to borrow it; comedy says mūtuom argentum (Plaut. Trin. 758). A thing lent to be used and given back is given ūtendum (see borrow).

terms.gloss: a loan, as the lender sees it
evidence: Sall. Cat. 25.4: crēditum abjūrāverat, she had denied a loan on oath
Cato Agr. 5.4: injussū dominī crēdat nēminī, let him lend to no one without the master’s leave
terms.comment: From crēdere, to lend, to trust someone with money (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: sī quoi mūtuom quid dederis, fit prō propriō perditum: quom repetās, inimīcum amīcum beneficiō inveniās tuō.
phrases.english: Lend anybody anything and it is as good as lost: when you ask for it back, you find that your kindness has made your friend an enemy.

phrases.latin: Age, sequere mē, dabō tibi mūtuō jūglandēs. — Amīcē nunc loqueris. Sed quandō reddam? — Ad Kalendās Graecās, sī nōn potes citius.
phrases.english: Come on, follow me, I’ll lend you some walnuts. — Now you’re talking like a friend. But when do I give them back? — On the Greek Kalends, if you can’t sooner.

phrases.latin: nūllus est tibi quem rogēs mūtuom argentum
phrases.english: you have no one to ask for a loan of money
